questions.question: A partnership deed does NOT necessarily include which of the following?
options: A) Date of formation of the firm
B) Method of calculating profit share
C) Interest on capital rate, if any
D) Name and address of the firm
questions.explanation: A partnership deed may contain many clauses, but the exact date of formation is not a mandatory clause. Other clauses like the firm's name, profit-sharing ratio, and interest on capital are commonly included.

questions.question: Under the fluctuating capital method, which of the following items is recorded in the partner's capital account?
options: B) All adjustments like salary, interest on capital, and drawings
questions.explanation: Under fluctuating capital method, all appropriations (salary, interest on capital, share of profit, drawings) are recorded in the capital account, causing the capital balance to fluctuate.

questions.question: Interest on partner's drawings is recorded on the ____ side of the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account.
questions.explanation: Interest on drawings is an income for the firm (charged from partners), so it appears on the credit side of the P&L Appropriation Account.

questions.question: If a partner's share was under-distributed in the past, the rectifying entry would involve:
options: A) Only crediting the partner who received less
C) Debiting the partner who received excess and crediting the partner who received less
questions.explanation: The partner who received more than their correct share is debited, and the partner who received less is credited to rectify the error.

questions.question: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account is prepared after which account?
questions.explanation: P&L Appropriation Account is an extension of the P&L Account. First, the P&L Account determines net profit/loss, then appropriations are shown in the P&L Appropriation Account.

questions.question: Under the fixed capital method, partner's drawings are recorded in a separate account called:
questions.explanation: Under fixed capital method, drawings are debited to a separate Drawings Account (or Current Account), not the Capital Account, so that capital remains fixed.

questions.question: A, B, and C are partners sharing profits in the ratio 3:2:1. If the total profit is ₹60,000, how much will C receive?
questions.explanation: C's share = ₹60,000 × 1/6 = ₹10,000. The ratio 3:2:1 means total parts = 6, so C gets 1/6 of the profit.

questions.question: X and Y are partners. X guarantees that Z's share of profit will not be less than ₹40,000 per annum. If the firm incurs a loss of ₹20,000, what is the amount of deficiency to be borne by X?
questions.explanation: Z's guaranteed minimum is ₹40,000. Since there's a loss of ₹20,000, Z's actual share is negative ₹20,000. Deficiency = ₹40,000 + ₹20,000 = ₹60,000, which X must bear.

questions.question: When a new partner is admitted, the sacrificing ratio is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Sacrificing ratio = Old profit share − New profit share. It represents the portion of profit each old partner gives up in favor of the new partner.

questions.question: The goodwill of a firm is valued at ₹90,000. A new partner brings ₹15,000 as goodwill premium. The remaining goodwill amount will be:
options: A) Shown as an asset in the balance sheet
B) Debited to new partner's capital account
C) Credited to all partners equally
D) Credited to old partners' capital accounts in sacrificing ratio
questions.explanation: The remaining goodwill (₹90,000 − ₹15,000 = ₹75,000) is credited to old partners' capital accounts in their sacrificing ratio to compensate them for their sacrifice.

questions.question: An increase in the value of assets at the time of admission of a partner is recorded in the Revaluation Account as:
options: A) Shown in Balance Sheet directly
D) Not recorded in Revaluation Account
questions.explanation: Increase in asset value is a gain, so it is credited to the Revaluation Account. Decrease in asset value or increase in liability is debited.

questions.question: When a new partner is admitted, the existing partners' capital accounts are adjusted for goodwill through:
options: B) Raising and writing off goodwill or premium method
C) Journal entry only in cash book
D) Adjusting only the new partner's account
questions.explanation: There are two common methods: (1) Premium method — goodwill brought in by new partner is distributed to old partners; (2) Memorandum revaluation/raising method.

questions.question: Capitalisation of average profit method of goodwill valuation uses which formula?
options: A) Goodwill = Capitalised Value − Net Assets
questions.explanation: Capitalisation of average profit: Goodwill = (Average Profit / Normal Rate of Return) − Net Assets. The first term is the capitalised value of the business.

questions.question: A, B, and C share profits equally (1:1:1). A retires. B and C acquire A's share in the ratio 2:1. What is the gaining ratio of B and C?
questions.explanation: Since A retires, B and C acquire A's share (1/3) in the ratio 2:1 as given. Gaining ratio = 2:1.

questions.question: A firm's average profit is ₹50,000. Normal rate of return is 10%. Capital employed is ₹4,00,000. What is goodwill under the super profit method if years of purchase is 3?
At the time of retirement of a partner, the gaining ratio is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Gaining ratio = New profit share − Old profit share. It represents how much the remaining partners gain from the retiring partner's share.

questions.question: On dissolution of a firm, which account is prepared to record the sale of assets and payment of liabilities?
questions.explanation: Realisation Account is prepared at dissolution to record the realization (sale) of assets and settlement of liabilities.

questions.question: When assets are transferred to Realisation Account, the entry is:
options: A) Debit Realisation Account, Credit Asset Account
B) Debit Asset Account, Credit Realisation Account
C) Debit Realisation Account, Credit Capital Account
D) Debit Cash Account, Credit Realisation Account
questions.explanation: Assets are transferred by debiting Realisation Account (to record disposal) and crediting the individual Asset Account (to remove it from books).

questions.question: The correct order of payment on dissolution of a firm is:
options: B) Partners' loans → Outside debts → Partners' capital
C) Outside debts → Partners' loans → Partners' capital
D) Partners' capital → Partners' loans → Outside debts
questions.explanation: The order is: (1) Outside creditors, (2) Partners' loans, (3) Partners' capital (surplus, if any).

questions.question: A firm has assets of ₹5,00,000 and liabilities of ₹2,00,000. Assets are sold for ₹4,20,000 and liabilities paid at book value. What is the profit/loss on realisation?
questions.explanation: Book value of assets = ₹5,00,000. Sale proceeds = ₹4,20,000. Loss = ₹5,00,000 − ₹4,20,000 = ₹80,000. Liabilities paid at book value = no effect.

questions.question: If the Realisation Account shows a debit balance, it indicates:
options: B) Assets sold at book value
questions.explanation: Debit balance in Realisation Account = total debits (assets transferred, realisation expenses) > total credits (liabilities transferred, sale proceeds) → loss.

questions.question: Partners X and Y share profits 3:2. On dissolution, realisation loss is ₹25,000. How much loss does Y bear?
questions.explanation: Realisation loss is shared in the profit-sharing ratio. Y's share = ₹25,000 × 2/5 = ₹10,000.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT recorded in the Realisation Account?
options: C) Partner's salary for the past year
questions.explanation: Past year's partner salary relates to earlier periods and is not part of the dissolution process. Only transactions related to asset disposal, liability settlement, and dissolution expenses go through Realisation Account.

questions.question: When shares are issued at a price higher than face value, the excess amount is called:
questions.explanation: When shares are issued at a premium, the amount over face value is credited to Securities Premium Account.

questions.question: Which account is debited when shares are forfeited?
questions.explanation: When shares are forfeited, Share Capital Account is debited with the called-up value to cancel the shares, and allotment/call accounts are credited.

questions.question: Shares originally issued at a premium can be re-issued at:
options: A) Only at a price higher than face value
C) Any price not less than the unpaid amount
D) Only at the original issue price
questions.explanation: Forfeited shares can be re-issued at par, premium, or even at a discount (limited to the amount forfeited on those shares). The discount on re-issue cannot exceed the amount credited to Share Forfeiture Account.

questions.question: A shareholder holding 200 shares of ₹10 each (issued at par) fails to pay ₹3 on allotment and ₹2 on first call. If the shares are forfeited, what amount is debited to Share Capital Account?
questions.explanation: Called-up value per share = ₹10 (full). Share Capital Account is debited with the called-up value = 200 × ₹10 = ₹2,000. The unpaid amount (allotment ₹3 + call ₹2 = ₹5 per share) is credited to respective call accounts.

questions.question: Debentures issued at a discount are recorded in the books as:
options: A) Debit Discount on Issue of Debentures Account
B) Debit Premium on Issue of Debentures Account
C) Credit Discount on Issue of Debentures Account
questions.explanation: Discount on issue of debentures is a capital loss. It is debited to Discount on Issue of Debentures Account and is written off over the life of debentures.

questions.question: Application money received on share issue is initially credited to:
questions.explanation: Application money is credited to Share Application Account. On allotment, it is transferred from Share Application to Share Capital Account.

questions.question: Interest on debentures is charged against:
questions.explanation: Interest on debentures is a charge against profits and is debited to Profit and Loss Account, not an appropriation of profit.

questions.question: 100 shares of ₹10 each (issued at ₹12 premium) were forfeited after the shareholder failed to pay ₹5 (final call including ₹2 premium). These shares were re-issued at ₹8 per share fully paid. What is the balance in Share Forfeiture Account after re-issue?
questions.explanation: Total amount paid per share = ₹10 (face) + ₹12 (premium) − ₹5 (unpaid) = ₹17. Total forfeited = ₹17 × 100 = ₹1,700. Re-issue at ₹8, discount from face value ₹10 = ₹2 × 100 = ₹200. Share Forfeiture balance after re-issue = ₹1,700 − ₹200 = ₹1,500 (transferred to Capital Reserve).

questions.question: X Ltd. forfeited 50 shares of ₹100 each (issued at 10% premium) on which ₹40 (including premium of ₹10) on allotment and ₹30 on first call were not paid. The shares were re-issued as ₹80 paid-up for ₹70 per share. What is the amount transferred to Capital Reserve?
questions.explanation: Share of ₹100, issued at ₹110 (10% premium). Application = ₹30 (unpaid: allotment ₹40 + first call ₹30 + final call ₹40 = ₹110 total). Amount paid = Application ₹30 × 50 = ₹1,500. Re-issue as ₹80 paid-up at ₹70/share: discount = ₹80 − ₹70 = ₹10 × 50 = ₹500. Capital Reserve = ₹1,500 − ₹500 = ₹1,000.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a part of the financial statements as per Schedule III of the Companies Act, 2013?
options: C) Statement of Profit and Loss
questions.explanation: Trial Balance is an internal document, not a published financial statement. The main financial statements are Balance Sheet, P&L, Cash Flow Statement, and Notes to Accounts.

questions.question: In a comparative income statement, each item is expressed as a percentage of:
options: C) Net sales/revenue of the respective year
questions.explanation: In a comparative (common size) income statement, each item is shown as a percentage of net sales/revenue from operations of that year.

questions.question: Current ratio is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Current Ratio = Current Assets ÷ Current Liabilities. It measures the firm's ability to meet short-term obligations.

questions.question: Gross profit ratio is calculated on the basis of:
questions.explanation: Gross Profit Ratio = (Gross Profit / Net Sales) × 100. Gross Profit = Net Sales − Cost of Goods Sold.

questions.question: Debt-Equity ratio is classified as a:
questions.explanation: Debt-Equity Ratio measures the firm's long-term solvency by comparing long-term debt to shareholders' funds.

questions.question: Purchase of machinery for cash is classified under which activity in the Cash Flow Statement?
questions.explanation: Purchase of fixed assets (machinery) is an investing activity in the cash flow statement.

questions.question: A company's current assets are ₹4,00,000, inventory is ₹1,00,000, and current liabilities are ₹2,00,000. What is the quick ratio?
questions.explanation: Quick Assets = Current Assets − Inventory = ₹4,00,000 − ₹1,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Quick Ratio = ₹3,00,000 / ₹2,00,000 = 1.5:1.

questions.question: A fixed asset originally costing ₹5,00,000 with accumulated depreciation of ₹2,00,000 is sold for ₹3,50,000. How is this transaction reflected in the Cash Flow Statement under the indirect method?
options: A) Investing inflow ₹3,50,000; profit of ₹50,000 deducted from operating activities
C) Investing inflow ₹3,50,000; profit of ₹50,000 added to operating activities
questions.explanation: Book value = ₹5,00,000 − ₹2,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Sold for ₹3,50,000 → profit ₹50,000. Under indirect method: full ₹3,50,000 is investing inflow; the ₹50,000 profit (non-operating income) is deducted from net profit in operating activities section.

questions.question: A company has current assets of Rs.8,00,000 and current liabilities of Rs.3,20,000. What is the current ratio?
Which of the following is NOT a feature of a Computerised Accounting System?
questions.explanation: CAS processes transactions electronically. While entries are input by users, the processing, posting, and report generation are automated. 'Manual journal entries only' is not a feature.

questions.question: In MS Excel, which function is used to calculate the sum of a range of cells?
questions.explanation: SUM() function adds all numbers in a specified range of cells. AVERAGE() calculates mean, COUNT() counts cells with numbers, MAX() finds the largest value.

questions.question: Which Excel function is used to calculate depreciation using the Straight Line Method?
questions.explanation: SLN(cost, salvage, life) calculates straight-line depreciation. DB = declining balance, DDB = double-declining balance, VDB = variable declining balance.

questions.question: In Excel, the PMT() function is used to:
options: B) Calculate periodic payment for a loan
questions.explanation: PMT(rate, nper, pv) calculates the periodic payment for a loan based on constant payments and constant interest rate.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key component of a payroll schedule?
options: C) Gross pay, deductions, and net pay
questions.explanation: A payroll schedule includes all components: gross pay (basic + allowances), deductions (tax, PF, etc.), and net pay (take-home amount).

questions.question: In Excel, which chart type is most suitable for showing the composition (parts) of a whole?
questions.explanation: A pie chart is best suited for showing how parts make up a whole (composition). Line charts show trends, bar charts compare values, scatter charts show relationships.

questions.question: In Excel, if you want to keep a cell reference constant when copying a formula, you use:
questions.explanation: Absolute reference (e.g., $A$1) keeps the cell reference fixed when the formula is copied to other cells. Relative reference (A1) changes automatically.

questions.question: Which of the following software is commonly used as a Computerised Accounting System?
questions.explanation: Tally is a widely used accounting software. The others are word processor, image editor, and web browser respectively.

questions.question: The formula for straight-line depreciation per year is:
questions.explanation: Straight-line depreciation = (Original Cost − Estimated Salvage Value) ÷ Estimated Useful Life. It allocates equal depreciation each year.
